subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: When I, Nirmala, was in Class 6, my group in Dumdum had a fight over the science exhibit. Two of us wanted a clay model of a volcano, and two of us were sure a big poster would win the prize. We argued for two days, Disha. Then Meenal, the quietest one, said, "Why not both?" We made a poster showing how volcanoes form, with a little model that moved in the middle. The modellers glued the clay, the drawers coloured the poster, and both sides got the part they cared for. We came second in the exhibition, and nobody sulked at all.

qa.q: How long did the group in Dumdum argue?
qa.a: The group argued for two days.

qa.q: What did Meenal want, and how might Meenal have felt, when saying, "Why not both?"
qa.a: Meenal was probably tired of the two-day argument and hopeful that a plan keeping both ideas would end it without either side losing.

qa.q: What choice inside the story ended the argument, and why did it work?
qa.a: The choice to make a poster with a small model worked because both sides kept the part they cared about.

qa.q: How did Meenal's idea look to the two sides who had been arguing?
qa.a: Both sides could see their own idea in the plan, so nobody felt they had lost; the result was that nobody sulked.

grounding: Two children want a model and two want a poster, and the group combines them into one plan so each keeps the part they care about.

subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: The windmill project was due in two days, and the group was split down the middle. Shreya and Kiran wanted a model; Tushar and Anjali wanted a poster. They had one evening and only the materials in Shreya's house. "A model looks better," Kiran said. "A poster explains more," said Tushar. Shreya stared at the chart paper and the ice-cream sticks on the floor. "What if... it's a poster, with all the explaining, and a small windmill stuck on it that really turns?" Tushar tilted his head. "Only small?" "Palm-sized. Pinned in the corner." By nine the poster was done, and when you blew on the corner, the little windmill spun.

qa.q: What was Shreya thinking as she stared at the chart paper and sticks?
qa.a: She was looking for a way to satisfy both halves, and felt hopeful when the idea of a poster with a small windmill came.

qa.q: Why did mixing the ideas work better than choosing one?
qa.a: Both pairs kept what they cared about, the explaining and the moving model, so nobody felt they had lost.

qa.q: How might Tushar see the final poster?
qa.a: Tushar wanted a poster that explains and got one, with a little windmill he could accept, so he'd likely be satisfied.

grounding: Shows a split group combining ideas into a poster with a small turning windmill attached, so both sides keep what they care about.

subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: In Nazia's flat in Pune, the four of them had been arguing since lunch. Binita and Nazia wanted a poster about the water cycle, with arrows and labels. The two boys wanted a model, with real water. Binita sat back and thought out loud. "Why do you want a model?" "Because it moves. It's not boring." "And we want a poster because it explains everything." She looked at the empty chart paper. "So what if we make the poster, and stick a small model on it? A little plastic-cup cloud that tips and drips into a bottle-cap sea?" The boys looked at each other. "Moving part?" "Moving part." Nazia was already drawing the arrows.

qa.q: What would the small model on the poster be?
qa.a: A little plastic-cup cloud that tips and drips into a bottle-cap sea.

qa.q: Why did Binita ask the boys why they wanted a model?
qa.a: She was curious about what mattered to them, hoping to find a plan both sides would be happy with.
She found what each side cared about, movement and explaining, and put both into one plan.

qa.q: How might the two boys feel about the new plan?
qa.a: They get their moving part, so they would likely feel heard and keen to build it.

grounding: Illustrates two pairs who want a model or a poster agreeing on a poster with a small moving model attached, so each keeps what matters to them.
